headline: Deer Island to Graves: bass shadow bunker on the Harvest Moon push
subhead: Bigger tides are moving bigger bait through the harbor's channels, and the fleet is finally seeing the fall pattern take shape from Winthrop to Gloucester.
body_markdown:
If you've only got two or three days this week, point the bow toward the harbor islands before you run north to the rocks. That's the call, and here's the reasoning behind it. The Harvest Moon tides that peaked over the weekend are still running big, and big tides mean more current through the gaps between Deer Island, Long Island, and Spectacle Island — current that's now loaded with adult bunker and the last of the summer mackerel schools getting pushed through on schedule. We flagged this exact setup last week — said blitz-style feeding would get more frequent as bait kept concentrating — and that's exactly what's showing up on the VHF chatter out of Winthrop and Hull this week.

The bunker schools are thick enough now that you can find them by the birds alone. Terns and gulls are working pods off Deer Island Light on the last two hours of the incoming, and where the bait balls tighten up against the rip lines off the Deer Island flats, stripers are punching through from underneath. Nothing sustained yet — this isn't a wall-to-wall blitz — but it's real, repeatable action for anyone willing to idle and watch before committing. Live-lined bunker on a 5/0 circle hook, no weight, just enough leader to keep it natural, has been the top producer in that 15-to-25-foot depth range on the edge of the channel. If you don't want to net your own bait, snag-and-drop still works fine once you find the pods stacked tight.

Spectacle Island's north side is holding a similar pattern on the dropping tide, with bass working the ledge in 20 feet where the bottom falls off hard toward the shipping channel. Bucktails in the 1.5 to 2-ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked with a slow lift-and-drop along that edge, have been taking fish in the 28-to-34-inch range — mostly schoolies and a scattering of slot fish, nothing huge yet, but consistent enough that a few boats are making it a daily stop.

Up on the North Shore, Nahant and the rocks around East Point are fishing the way they should this time of year — better at first light and again in the last hour before dark, with poppers and pencil poppers drawing surface strikes from bass working bait pinned against the ledges. The rocky structure off Bass Rocks and Eastern Point in Gloucester is holding a similar bite, though the reports out of Cape Ann this week have been mixed — some mornings stacked with fish chasing peanut bunker into the wash, other mornings dead calm with nothing showing until the tide turns. That inconsistency tracks with what's happening offshore: the warm-water signature that's been sitting off southern New England all month hasn't broken down yet, so bait movement through Cape Ann is still patchy rather than a steady conveyor.

Bluefish are riding along with the bunker wherever it shows up, and they're not shy about it. Choppers in the 3-to-6-pound class are cutting through peanut schools off Winthrop and Deer Island on wire leader and diamond jigs, and anyone throwing metal without a shock tippet is going home short baits. The bluefish bite tends to be the tell — where you find aggressive blues slashing the surface, stripers are usually stacked underneath working the same bait from below. Watch for that pattern to intensify over the next week as more forage gets pushed south and east ahead of the seasonal cool-down; the bluefish are the leading edge of that push right now.

South toward Plymouth and Duxbury Bay, the flounder bite on the flats has been steady on sandworms and clam strips fished on the bottom during the last of the ebb, when the water pulls off the mud and concentrates fish in the deeper guts. Nothing spectacular in size — most fish running 12 to 14 inches — but it's a dependable fallback if the striper bite up north goes quiet on a given tide. Scituate's ledges are still holding some resident bass working the rock piles on the outgoing, best fished with a 3/4-ounce bucktail tipped with a Fin-S trailer, worked tight to the structure rather than out in open water.

Weather-wise, the wind pattern this week has stayed manageable — nothing shutting down the harbor, but a stiff northeast blow midweek could roughen up the outer islands and push the bite tighter into protected water like the inner harbor channels and Duxbury Bay. If that happens, shift effort to Deer Island and Spectacle Island rather than fighting chop off Nahant or Gloucester.

Looking ahead, the next few days should keep building on this pattern rather than backing off. The bigger tides aren't done yet, bait is still funneling through the harbor on schedule, and the bluefish activity suggests more bunker is stacking up behind what's already here. If there's only one window to fish this week, make it the dropping tide at Deer Island or Spectacle Island in the two hours before and after the moon-driven high — that's where the current, the bait, and the fish are lining up most reliably right now. Keep Nahant and Gloucester as the early and late-light option, and don't count out Plymouth's flounder bite as insurance if the bigger fish go quiet on any given tide.
